newsitem.title: UK: UK budget -- background, options, forecasts.
newsitem.headline: UK budget -- background, options, forecasts.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown is set to target both the consumer and the corporate sector for tax rises in his first budget on July 2, financial analysts believe.

A steady stream of apparent leaks to newspapers has persuaded economists that the housing market could face a double hit, aimed particularly at the better-off, while the corporate sector should see reduced tax breaks on share dividend payments as well as the long-awaited "windfall tax" on privatised utilities.
Brown is also likely to introduce a package of "green" measures and to increase taxes on cigarettes.

His main aims are to prevent the frisky consumer sector from causing an unsustainable economic boom, encourage companies to spend more on investment and get some of the long-term unemployed back to work.
Brown will restate his intention of introducing a new bottom rate of income tax of 10 percent, half the current starting rate, but will hold off on implementing it, analysts believe.
Brown will begin his budget speech in the House of Commons at 1430 GMT on Wednesday.
Following is a summary of the economic background and the main tax changes and economic forecasts expected in the budget:
PRIVATE SECTOR

The consumer sector is enjoying a spending and borrowing boom, fuelled in particular by "windfall" payments to millions of Britons totalling around 30 billion stg from building society mergers and flotations.

If the Chancellor does not aim some tax increases at the private sector, analysts believe the Bank of England will increase official interest rates aggressively from the current 6.5 percent, in a bid to ensure the country hits its inflation target. Interest rate bears see rates heading up to 8.0 percent.

Earlier newspaper reports suggested Prime Minister Tony Blair had vetoed a reduction in tax relief on mortgage interest (MIRAS), fearing it would look as if his Labour Party, which returned to power in May after 18 years in opposition, was reneging on the spirit of its election pledge not to raise income tax.
The surge in house prices and the strength of recent economic data are now thought to have changed Blair's mind and some reduction in MIRAS, if not its outright abolition, is now widely expected.
Weekend press speculation suggested Brown would reduce MIRAS, which gives a tax break on the first 30,000 stg on mortgages, to 10 percent from 15 percent.
The change should garner some 900 million stg for the Treasury, at a cost to each of Britain's 10 million homeowners of up to 10 stg per month.

A survey from Nationwide building society on Friday sparked fears that the new confidence in the housing market could fuel inflation pressures in the rest of the economy. June house prices rose by an annual 11.0 percent, their strongest rise since the third quarter of 1989.

Brown is also thought likely to increase stamp duty on property transactions at the top end of the market to around 2.0 percent. Stamp duty is currently levied at a flat rate of one percent on homes worth 60,000 stg or more.
ENVIRONMENTAL MEASURES
Following last week's earth summit, the budget is likely to have a distinct "green" bias with measures aimed at helping reduce emissions which are causing global warming.

A big rise in fuel excise duty, perhaps of three pence per litre is thought to be on the agenda. Company car and car-parking perks may also be hit. Insurance tax on motor policies is expected to rise to 17.5 percent from four percent.

Brown has already pledged to cut value added tax (VAT) to five percent from eight percent on domestic fuel consumption, which some commentators fear could encourage extra energy consumption. To offset this, Brown is expected to cut VAT on loft insulation, which helps reduce energy use, to five from eight percent as well.
EXCISE DUTIES

The budget is likely to contain further hefty increases in taxes on cigarettes, perhaps as much as 10p per packet. Beer duty may fall to compete with cheap beer from continental Europe, where duty is lower, but "alcopops" such as alcoholic lemonades may be surcharged.
CORPORATE SECTOR
ADVANCE CORPORATION TAX (ACT)
Most commentators now expect gradual abolition of ACT which gives tax breaks for dividend payments on shares. The current rate is 20 percent and this is expected to be reduced to 15 or 10 percent.

Halving the rate would save the Treasury around 3.0 billion stg. The move could be presented as a way of encouraging firms to invest more of their profits rather than giving them away to shareholders.
Other measures to encourage investment are also likely, with the possibility of the phased introduction of generous capital allowances for investment and research and development.
WINDFALL TAX

Brown is expected to raise around 5.0 billion stg from what he views as excess profits from privatised utility companies. Three billion stg of the money will be used to finance a welfare-to-work scheme to help the young long-term unemployed.
ECONOMY
GROWTH

Revised first quarter data for UK gross domestic product (GDP) showed the economy grew 0.9 percent compared with the fourth quarter of 1996 and at an annual rate of 3.1 percent, well above the trend rate of 2.25 to 2.5 percent. The economy is now in its sixth straight year of economic growth.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect Brown to predict GDP growth of 3.5 percent for 1997, compared with a 2.5 percent rise in 1996.

The consumer sector continues to be the main engine of growth, with manufacturing sluggish because of slow economic growth in continental Europe and also on the back of weakening export demand as sterling continues its bull run.
Commentators are warning that if interest rates rather than taxes are used to take the heat out of the economy, sterling will remain high, exacerbating the problem for exporters.
INFLATION
Brown is expected to forecast retail price inflation excluding mortgage interest payments (RPIX) still on target at 2.5 percent by the end of the year.
The Bank of England, which is responsible for keeping inflation under control, has warned that the consumer sector represents a threat to the inflation outlook.

British interest rates have been increased by 1/4 point in each of the past two months and some economists are looking for a further rise on July 10, at the end of the monetary policy committee's next meeting.
GOVERNMENT FINANCES

Brown is likely to announce a net fiscal tightening of 4.0 billion stg, according to a Reuters poll of 20 economists last week, but expectations are starting to inch up as the extent of the consumer boom becomes more apparent.
Brown is expected to predict a 1997-98 deficit of just 16.0 billion stg, down from around 23 billion in 1996-97. This would be the lowest deficit for six years.

By 1998-99, there is even better news, with the deficit poised to tumble to just 12.0 billion stg. Some analysts are saying it could even be as low as five billion stg as the strength of the economy increases the government's tax take.

There is some concern that Britain is not yet posting a surplus, despite six years of economic recovery, and that Labour is still some way from hitting its "golden rule" of only borrowing to finance investment -- around one percent of GDP.
But the country is set to meet the EU single currency requirement of a public sector deficit which does not exceed 3.0 percent of GDP.
